_: THE CLOSED TABLE. Every name a user-authored formula may call, and there is no other list. DATA, not code, because BOTH lanes read it -- app/src/components/chart/engine/ast/parse.js configures the parser from it and api/services/ast_interpret.py walks the tree it produces. A hand-copy in either lane would be a second grammar, and this repo has already measured what two vocabularies cost: `williams_r` here is `williamsR` in the chart registry, which is why `_CASE_COLUMNS` exists at all.
_shape: FOUR sections. `series` maps a bar-field name to the key it reads. `operators` maps an operator name to its arity -- the canonical tree spells unary minus `u-` and the ternary `?:`, and those names ARE the operator names, not a rendering of them. The functions section maps a name to its argument kinds, its lookback declaration and its read-back sentence. `scalars` maps a per-symbol name to the stored column it reads, the column that DATES it, and its cadence. Every entry in the last three also declares `yields`.
_canonical: The parse->canonical boundary is where this table closes. The persisted tree has FIVE node types -- num, series, op, call, offset -- with keys drawn from {type, name, value, args} and nothing else, so a Python walker has five cases and a surface small enough to prove closed. Anything jsep can produce that has no canonical form (a member read, an array, `this`, a compound, a call of a call) is refused BY NAME at that boundary. ⭐ THE FIFTH ADDED NO KEY. An `offset` node is `{type, value, args}` with NO `name`, so the vocabulary above is exactly the one it was, and every walker in both lanes reaches the child through the `node.args` descent it already had -- which means a walker that has never heard of `offset` reports the CHILD's contribution rather than silently dropping the subtree. See `_no_offset` for the whole of what that node may say. ⚰️ THIS SAID *"FOUR node types -- num, series, op, call"*, and it was right from v1 until `291c9d8a` landed the bounded backward offset on 2026-08-09; the sentence outlived the grammar by part of a day and would have outlived it indefinitely, because nothing was checking it. It is no longer hand-maintained: `closedTable.test.js` composes this claim from `parse.js::NODE_TYPES` and fails BY NAME the day a sixth type lands. A count typed beside the list it describes is this repo's most repeated defect.
_no_offset: ⭐ THERE IS A BOUNDED BACKWARD OFFSET, AND IT IS SHAPED SO THAT A FORWARD ONE STAYS UNSAYABLE. `expr[n]` reads `expr` n bars before the bar being written, and it canonicalises to `{ type: 'offset', value: <integer >= 1>, args: [ <any canonical node> ] }`. There is NO `name` key, and `args` is reused rather than a new key invented, so the child is reached by the `node.args` descent every walker in both lanes already performs. ⭐ THE CHILD IS ANY EXPRESSION, NOT ONLY A BAR FIELD -- `sma(close, 20)[2]`, `(close > open)[1]` and `market_cap[1]` are all legal. That was measured, not assumed: in a corpus of 54 real Pine scripts the offset is most often taken of a call result or a named intermediate, so a series-only form would have covered about half of real usage at exactly the same lookback cost. ⛔ `[0]` FOLDS TO THE BARE CHILD at the parse door, so a zero-bar node never persists and `x[0]` and `x` can never become two `astHash`es for one column. FIVE GUARDS, PAIRWISE DISJOINT, four at the parse door and one on the stored tree: `canonicalise:offset-forward` for a negative bar count, `canonicalise:offset-literal` for anything that is not a plain whole number, `canonicalise:offset-chained` for a second application, `canonicalise:member` for `close.foo` and `close["constructor"]` -- THE LITERAL KIND IS WHAT DECIDES, a string being a property NAME and a number a bar INDEX -- and `interpret:offset` for a stored tree that was hand-written rather than parsed. ⛔ AND NO CEILING AMONG THEM, DELIBERATELY. `close[100000]` is a well-formed backward offset; what refuses it is `budget:lookback`, because an offset is counted by the same tree sum `sma(close, 600)` is. A second limit here would be a number nobody could re-derive, and the two would drift. ⭐ THE ORIGINAL RESTRICTION STILL HOLDS IN SPIRIT, WHICH IS THE ONLY REASON IT COULD BE GRANTED. A FORWARD REFERENCE REMAINS INEXPRESSIBLE: the sign is refused AT PARSE, the value must be a literal, and the node has NO SLOT for an expression that could evaluate negative -- so "the offset is a constant" is true BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by a check somebody can delete. maxLookback(ast) is therefore STILL A TREE SUM and never became a dataflow analysis: an offset contributes `back = value + child.back` and leaves `forward = child.forward` untouched. Measured: `close[2]` is 2, `sma(close[2], 20)` is 22, `sma(ema(close[1],5)[2], 20)` is 28, and `ichimokuChikou(high, low, close, 9, 26, 52)[3]` reads back 55 / forward 26 -- the offset moved the back and left the forward exactly where the manifest declared it. ⛔ THE CHAIN IS REFUSED FOR A STRONGER REASON THAN PINE'S BAN ON IT. `close[1][2]` and `close[3]` are the SAME COLUMN -- identical values, identical NaN prefix, identical maxLookback -- so admitting both would give one column TWO `astHash`es, and that hash is what decides whether an edit force-migrates every binding and resets `last_value`. Pine forbids the chain in its own grammar and the 54-script corpus contains none, so refusing it costs nothing; but the reason to refuse it here would stand even if Pine allowed it. ⭐ AND `ichimoku.chikou` -- THE VERY CONSTRUCTION THIS NOTE ONCE CITED AS THE REASON OFFSETS WERE FORBIDDEN -- NOW SHIPS, DECIDED. `ichimokuChikou` declares `forward: arg4` above; the linter reads that ONE declaration, `modeFromReach` returns `preview-repaints`, and the plot lints decidability `decided` with forward 26. That is this note's own argument reaching its conclusion rather than being abandoned: the linter stayed simple enough to be obviously right on the day it decides the brand's central claim, so the construction it exists to decide became DECLARABLE instead of forbidden. ⚰️ THIS SAID *"THERE IS NO `ref`, NO `offset` AND NO BACKWARD-INDEX FORM IN v1, AND THAT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN AN OMISSION"*, because a general `close[n]` *"turns the repaint linter from a lookback SUM into a dataflow analysis, and it makes a FORWARD reference expressible in the first place -- the exact construction (`chikou[j] === close[j+26]`) that the repaint record already names as the thing the linter has to be able to decide."* BOTH REASONS WERE RIGHT, AND NEITHER COST WAS PAID -- what changed on 2026-08-09 (`291c9d8a`) is the SHAPE, not the ruling. The v1 text is kept verbatim rather than overwritten because it is what stops the GENERAL `close[n]`, the one that would still cost both, from being proposed again as though it had never been considered. ⚠️ THE RESERVATION IN `_no_offset_reopened_by` WAS HONOURED, NOT IGNORED. `291c9d8a` deliberately left this file untouched and named the stale note in its report instead of editing it; this rewrite is the manifest owner's own instruction to complete that build, taken with the repaint-claim owner's decision on `ichimoku.chikou` already recorded. Re-opening it FURTHER -- a computed offset, a signed one, or a chained one -- is still a SPEC decision belonging to those two owners together, and none of the three is a v2 feature request any later task may grant on its own.
_no_offset_reopened_by: Re-opening this is a SPEC decision, not an implementation one: it belongs to the owner of the repaint claim (spec section 4, the phase's repaint-linter task) plus the owner of this manifest, together, because it changes what the linter can decide and what both lane walkers must implement. It is not a v2 feature request that any later task may grant on its own.
_sentence: The read-back sentence lives HERE so that the chip's plain-English phrasing and the interpreter's dispatch come from ONE declaration. A read-back with its own phrase table is a second vocabulary in the same sense the note above describes. `{0}` and `{1}` are argument positions.
_functions_indicators: ⭐ THE INDICATORS ARE ORDINARY FUNCTIONS AND THEY TAKE THEIR INPUT SERIES EXPLICITLY. `atr(high, low, close, 14)` rather than `atr(14)`, and that is a decision `_no_offset` forces: an implicit-bars function would need a FIFTH argument kind and a walker that injects the bar array, and the arity every reader derives from `args.length` would stop being the arity the user types. Explicit series costs a longer call and buys three things — the arity check, the read-back and `maxLookback` all keep working with no reader changing, a Heikin-Ashi or a smoothed input is expressible (`atr(high, low, sma(close,3), 14)`), and `stoch(source, high, low, length)` is already the shape Pine uses. ⛔ AND NOT ONE LINE OF THE MATHS IS HERE OR IN EITHER WALKER: every entry below binds to the implementation the CHART already draws — `app/src/components/chart/indicators.js` in the browser and `api/services/indicator_compute.py` on the server — which are the two lanes `tests/fixtures/indicators/` already pins against each other at rel-tol 1e-9. A fifteenth RSI would be a second authority over one value, which is this repo's most repeated defect.
_functions_atr_convention: ⭐ `atr` IS WILDER'S, AND THE QUESTION WAS ASKED SERIOUSLY ENOUGH TO DESERVE A STANDING ANSWER. A sibling translator reported that our ATR *"matches neither Wilder RMA (0.20) nor SMA-of-TR (0.21) — a third convention"*, and raised it as a member-visible correctness defect because ATR feeds position sizing. It is not a third convention: `tests/test_ast_indicators.py::test_our_atr_IS_WILDER_and_the_difference_from_pine_is_the_SEED` builds Wilder's original independently — TR = max(h-l, |h-c[1]|, |l-c[1]|), seed = the simple mean of the first n TRs, then ATR_i = ATR_(i-1) + (TR_i - ATR_(i-1))/n — and the shipped column matches it to 5.4e-16 over 565 bars, while the simple-MA-of-TR alternative is asserted to DISAGREE so the match distinguishes something. ⛔ WHAT DIFFERS FROM PINE IS THE SEED, AND IT CONVERGES: Pine's `ta.tr` defines bar 0 as `high - low` (no previous close), so its TR series starts a bar earlier and `ta.rma`'s seed lands on bar n-1 where ours lands on bar n. Same smoothing, different first window — about 2.0e-2 apart at the seed, 3.0e-3 by bar 40, 2.8e-5 by bar 100, 1.3e-11 by bar 300. ⚠️ SO A CROSS-PRODUCT PROBE MUST NOT SAMPLE THE WARM-UP. `0.20` vs `0.21` read at bar 15 is two seeds, not two formulas, and reading it as a formula difference is how a correct implementation gets 'fixed'.
_functions_arg_roles: ⭐ EVERY FUNCTION NAMES ITS ARGUMENT POSITIONS, AND THAT IS FOR THE TRANSLATORS. `args` says a slot is a `series` or an `int`; it does NOT say WHICH series, and a translator turning `CCIx.z` or `ta.cci(src, len)` into a call has to know that slot 0 is the HIGH and slot 2 is the CLOSE. Guessing produces a NUMBER rather than a refusal, which is the worst failure shape this codebase has — a wrong answer that looks like an answer. ⛔ SO IT IS DATA, NOT PROSE. The PCF translator refused four whole families (`CCIx.z`, `DIPLUSd.z`, `DIMINUSd.z`, `WSTOCx.y.z`) because the order was only describable in a sentence, and a sentence is not something a parser can read. ⚠️ A ROLE IS NOT A REQUIREMENT. `atr`'s slot 0 is named `high` because that is what an untranslated call means, NOT because the argument must be the `high` series — `atr(high, low, sma(close,3), 14)` is legal and useful, and that composability is the whole reason the indicators take their series explicitly (see `_functions_indicators`). The role names what the maths EXPECTS there. ⭐ `period`-suffixed roles mark the `int` slots, so a translator can find the window without re-reading `args`; the two are asserted the same length and mutually consistent by `tests/test_ast_indicators.py`, so a slot renamed on one side and not the other lands RED rather than silently disagreeing.
_functions_warmup: ⚠️ `lookback` IS THE PER-BAR WINDOW, AND TWO SHIPPED IMPLEMENTATIONS ALSO CARRY A MINIMUM SERIES LENGTH. `plusDI`/`minusDI` first land on bar `period` — which is what `arg3` declares — but `computeADX`/`compute_adx_raw` return nothing at all for a series shorter than `2 * period`, and `rsi`/`mfi`/`atr` need `period + 1` bars to produce their bar-`period` value. The shortfall is inherited from the chart, it is IDENTICAL in both lanes, and its direction is extra NaN — never a wrong number — so it is stated here rather than encoded as a second lookback the linter would have to add to the tree sum. ⛔ A declaration that UNDER-states a window is the one thing a budget cannot use, so every entry below declares an argument that is an upper bound on its own warm-up whenever its periods are in the conventional order, and the walkers REFUSE the out-of-order call outright (see `_functions_domain`) rather than quietly under-declaring.
_functions_na: ⛔⛔ TWO ENTRIES DELIBERATELY BREAK THIS TABLE'S CENTRAL RULE, AND THEY ARE THE ONLY TWO. Everywhere else NaN means NOT COMPUTABLE and it PROPAGATES — a missing field is not a price of zero, and every guard in both walkers exists to keep a hole from becoming a confident number. `na` INSPECTS that state and `nz` REPLACES it, so neither propagates, and that is the whole reason they are worth naming here rather than leaving to a reader to infer from an implementation. ⭐ THEY ARE DECLARED BECAUSE THE ALTERNATIVE IS WORSE. Pine has both, real published scripts use them in about half of all cases, and a translator that cannot say `nz` either refuses those scripts or — far worse — silently drops the guard the author wrote, which turns their deliberate zero into our NaN and changes what their scan means. Declared, the choice is the USER'S and it is visible in the read-back. ⚠️ AND `nz(market_cap, 0) > 1e9` IS EXACTLY THE DEFECT `_scalars` WARNS ABOUT — a broken symbol wearing a quiet one's answer — which is now SAYABLE. That is a real cost, accepted knowingly: it is one function, it reads back in English as *"market cap where it is known, and 0 where it is not"*, and a member who writes it can see what they asked for. ⛔ `nz` TAKES ITS REPLACEMENT EXPLICITLY, with no one-argument form. Pine defaults the second argument to 0; this table does not, because a default zero is precisely the invisible half of the defect above. A translator supplies the literal, so the tree records what was meant. ⚠️ `na` YIELDS `bool`, so `na(x)` is a condition and `nz` is not — the two are not a pair of spellings for one idea.
_functions_rounding: ⚠️ `round` SPELLS ITS RULE OUT BECAUSE THE TWO LANGUAGES DISAGREE ABOUT IT. JavaScript's `Math.round` rounds a half UP (toward +∞, so -2.5 becomes -2) and Python's built-in `round` rounds a half to EVEN (2.5 and 3.5 both become 2 and 4). Neither matches the other and neither matches Pine, which rounds a half AWAY FROM ZERO. So both walkers compute `sign(x) * floor(abs(x) + 0.5)` — written out, not inherited — and `sign` is the same declared entry a formula can call. This is the same arrangement `min`/`max` already use for their NaN rule, and for the same reason: a divergence that appears only on exact halves is one no golden fixture would ever contain.
_functions_smoothing: ⭐ `rma` AND `ema` ARE ONE IMPLEMENTATION WITH TWO SMOOTHING CONSTANTS, IN BOTH LANES. Wilder's average is an exponential average with `alpha = 1 / n` where the ordinary one uses `2 / (n + 1)`; everything else — the seed (the mean of the first full window), the restart on a hole, the NaN prefix — is identical and must stay identical. Writing `rma` as its own loop would have been four lines and would have put a SECOND seeding rule in the table, which is how `rsi` and `atr` would come to disagree about the same average. ⚠️ `rma(x, n)` IS NOT `ema(x, 2n - 1)` HERE EVEN THOUGH THE ALGEBRA SAYS IT IS: that identity holds for the recurrence and not for the seed, because the seed averages `n` bars in one case and `2n - 1` in the other. The alpha is what is shared, never the period.
_functions_recurrence: ⭐ ONE ENTRY READS ITS OWN PREVIOUS VALUE, AND IT IS BOUNDED SO THAT THE ANSWER CANNOT DEPEND ON THE REQUEST. `accum(seed, update, warmup)` is the engine's bar-to-bar state: at bar `i` it seeds from `seed` at bar `i - warmup` and applies `update` once per bar across `(i - warmup, i]`, so the value at bar `i` is a function of exactly `warmup + 1` bars and NOTHING ELSE. ⭐⭐ THAT IS WHY IT IS SAFE, AND IT IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. A single forward pass from the first fetched bar would have been O(n) instead of O(n × warmup), and it would also have made `accum` mean a DIFFERENT NUMBER on a chart the user had panned — the exact defect `lesson_a_derived_value_must_not_depend_on_the_request` records (rolling values need a warm-up prefix; cumulative ones need an ABSOLUTE seed, and a window start is neither). The re-seeded window is window-independence BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by a check somebody can delete, and it is the same bargain every other rolling entry here already makes: `sma(close, 20)` is NaN for 19 bars and exact afterwards, and so is this. ⛔ SO THE PREFIX IS NaN, NEVER A SHORT ANSWER. Bars before `warmup` have no seed to run from, so they are NOT COMPUTABLE — never a partial accumulation, which would be a confident wrong number wearing a warm-up's clothes. ⭐ `recurrence` IS DATA BECAUSE FOUR READERS NEED IT: `seed`/`body`/`warmup` are ARGUMENT INDICES and `binds` is the reserved name the body reads its own past through, so no lane types the string `self` or the position `1`. The body at index `body` is the ONE argument in this whole table that is NOT evaluated eagerly to a column — it is a per-bar expression — and that asymmetry is declared here rather than living as folklore in two interpreters. ⛔ `binds` IS BOUND, NOT DECLARED: it is deliberately absent from the `series` section, so it never enters the sayable vocabulary, never needs a `field`, and resolving it anywhere outside a body fails through the scope lock that was already there. ⛔ AND THE BODY REACHES ITS OWN PAST THROUGH OPERATORS AND POINTWISE CALLS ONLY. `self` under an `offset`, under a windowed function, or inside a nested `accum` is refused BY NAME (`interpret:recurrence`), because the step loop holds ONE previous value and not a history — a walker that quietly read a column there would answer with the seed. Pointwise is DERIVED, never listed: an entry is pointwise iff its declared window is `lookback: 0` with no `forward` and no `int` argument, which is the same `ownWindow` reading the linter already performs. ⚠️ AND THE COST IS BOUNDED WHERE IT IS INCURRED: `warmup` is an `int` literal like every other window, so `budget:lookback` already caps it, and the product `bars × warmup` is refused by `interpret:steps` at evaluation time — the one cost this table cannot bound statically, because it is the only one that depends on how many bars the caller brought. ⚠️ `yields` IS `num`, DELIBERATELY, EVEN FOR A 0/1 ACCUMULATOR. `passthrough` resolves its arms as EVERY ARGUMENT AFTER THE FIRST (see `_yields`), which here would read the update AND the warm-up count — so a sticky flag is written `accum(...) > 0` and is a scan that way. Refusing to call a tree a scan costs an error message; admitting a real-valued tree as one makes `!= 0` true for every non-zero price on the board.
_functions_domain: ⛔ TWO ENTRIES HAVE AN ARGUMENT DOMAIN THE `int` KIND CANNOT EXPRESS, AND BOTH WALKERS ENFORCE IT THE SAME WAY — AS AN ALL-NaN COLUMN, NEVER AN EXCEPTION. `macd` declares `lookback: arg2`, which is only an upper bound while `slow >= fast`; `macd(close, 26, 12)` would compute its first value 14 bars later than the declaration promises, so it produces nothing instead. The Ichimoku five declare `lookback: arg4` (the senkou-B period) and every line of the shipped implementation starts there, so `max(tenkan, kijun) > senkouB` produces nothing. ⚠️ THE SECOND ONE IS ALSO A REAL CROSS-LANE DIVERGENCE THIS BINDING HAD TO CLOSE: `indicator_compute.compute_ichimoku_raw` already returns empty columns for it and `indicators.js::computeIchimoku` reads a NEGATIVE index and throws a TypeError. The guard is in both walkers' adapters, identically, so the two lanes agree — which is the whole reason it is written down here rather than left to whichever lane a caller happened to be in.
_booleans: There is no boolean node type, and the operators section is what forces that: it declares `!`, `&&`, `||` and `?:` over a table whose only literal is a number. A condition is therefore a 0/1 column, and the parser's `true`/`false` literals canonicalise to num 1 and num 0. Both lane walkers must agree on that, and it is asserted in parse.test.js rather than left to each lane to assume.
_yields: `yields` DECLARES WHAT AN ENTRY'S VALUES CAN BE -- `num`, `bool`, or `passthrough` on the ONE entry whose answer is the join of its branches (the ternary `?:`). It is here rather than in a reader because deciding whether a tree is a CONDITION -- a scan is `<ast> != 0` on a 0/1 column, see `_booleans` -- from a hand-list of `which operators are comparisons` is the list-that-rots shape, and it would be hand-listed TWICE, once per language. Declared here, `is_boolean_tree` is derived and a twelfth function is classified the day it lands. ⛔ THE THREE-VALUE SET IS NOT A WIDENING OF THE TWO THE CORRECTION ASKED FOR: `?:` has no static answer at all, and forcing it into `num` would refuse `(a > b) ? 1 : 0` as a scan while forcing it into `bool` would admit `x ? price : volume` as one. A reader that meets `passthrough` resolves it from the branches; a reader that meets an entry with NO `yields` must fail closed to `num`, because refusing to call a tree a scan costs a user an error message and admitting a real-valued tree as one makes `!= 0` true for every non-zero price on the board.
_scalars: A SCALAR IS A DIFFERENT KIND FROM A SERIES AND THE TABLE SAYS SO IN ITS OWN SECTION. `close` is a time series: one number per bar, and the number at bar i is a fact about bar i. `market_cap` is ONE NUMBER PER SYMBOL, dated to a nightly snapshot, and it is the SAME number at every bar of the column -- including at bars that closed before the snapshot was taken. Conflating them is the `chart_settings` vs `charts_workspace_layout` category error: two things with the same shape and different identities.
_scalars_node: A SCALAR RIDES THE `series` NODE TYPE RATHER THAN ADDING ONE OF ITS OWN. `parse.js` turns every identifier into a `series` node deliberately (so the parser needs no table) and resolution is `interpret`'s job; a `scalar` node type would be a NEW type in five declaration sites, and every stored tree's `astHash` is taken over `{type,...}` -- so adding one is a decision that can never be undone without a migration of every persisted definition. The linter already resolves a DECLARED SCALAR (a definition input) to reach (0,0); a table-declared scalar is the same shape with a wider declaration source. ⚰️ THIS OPENED *"…AND THE CANONICAL VOCABULARY STAYS FOUR"* and called a further type hypothetical (*"a FIFTH type… a fifth type is a decision that can never be undone"*), until `291c9d8a` added `offset` on 2026-08-09 and paid exactly the migration cost described above -- once, deliberately, and with the cost stated in advance. The ARGUMENT is unchanged and the arithmetic is not: a scalar still rides `series`, which is the part this note was always about. `_canonical` carries the live roster and `closedTable.test.js` derives it from `parse.js::NODE_TYPES`, so no count is restated here.
_scalars_as_of: `as_of` NAMES A COLUMN, NEVER A DATE. Freshness is PER SYMBOL -- one ticker's row can be a month older than another's -- so the declaration points at the row column that carries the value's own date. Two families exist and they are NOT the same date: fundamentals and ratings are dated by `snapshot_date` (when the build ran) and technicals, candles and patterns by `bars_asof` (the newest bar the maths saw). A single as-of would over-claim one family or under-claim the other. Which family each column belongs to is READ OFF `screener/snapshot_builder.build_row`, which sets `bars_asof` only inside the `if bars:` block that fills the technical, candle and pattern groups.
_scalars_freshness: ⭐ THE REPAINT LINTER RETURNS A TRUE ZERO HERE AND THAT IS WHY THERE IS A SECOND VERDICT. A scalar's value at bar i depends on no bar j > i, so `astReach` answers (0, 0) and the repaint gate PASSES `market_cap > 1e9` as non-repainting -- correctly, and uselessly. The zero is a true answer to a question nobody asked. `ast_freshness` / `freshness.js` ask the other one, off THIS section: `live` when no leaf is a scalar, `as-of-snapshot` when one is, `unknown` when a leaf declares something the reader cannot resolve. ⛔ IT IS A CADENCE CLAIM, NOT A STALENESS MEASUREMENT -- how fresh a given symbol's row IS is a per-row runtime fact read off the `as_of` column, and it belongs in a result envelope, never in a badge that would then depend on when it was rendered.
_scalars_totality: ⭐ `scalars` AND `_scalars_excluded` ARE A PARTITION OF `screener/snapshot_db.COLUMNS` -- their union is that list, they are disjoint, and both halves are required. A declared list without the excluded half is a list of what somebody remembered; with the identity, a 66th screener column lands RED until somebody DECIDES about it, which is the only thing that keeps this vocabulary honest as the screener grows. Measured 2026-08-09: 65 columns, 54 declared, 11 excluded. Every excluded entry states WHY, and eight of the eleven state the same reason -- the column is TEXT, and this table's only literal is a number (`_booleans`), so no expression over it is writeable at all.

_functions_excluded._: ⭐ THE INDICATORS THE CHART DRAWS THAT A FORMULA STILL CANNOT CALL, EACH WITH THE REASON. ⛔ EVERY KEY WITHOUT A LEADING UNDERSCORE IS A NAME A FORMULA MAY NOT SPELL, and a key WITH one is a note about the section; that split is load-bearing rather than cosmetic, because `conceptVocabulary.test.js` derives its undeclared-name probe from the non-underscore keys. Its probe used to be the literal `rsi`, which stopped being undeclared the day Phase F declared it -- a rail that went green by being overtaken. Declaring one of these means DELETING its key here, which moves the probe to the next refusal instead of silently leaving the rail pointing at a name that is now legal. Same identity `_scalars_excluded` carries and for the same reason: a declared list on its own is a list of what somebody remembered, and a member who cannot find `obv` deserves to know whether it was forgotten or refused. Every entry here was CONSIDERED against `_no_offset`'s rule — a lookback that is a constant or a named argument, so `maxLookback(ast)` stays a tree sum — and refused. ⛔ Adding one is not an implementation task: it either re-opens `_no_offset` (which `_no_offset_reopened_by` assigns to the owner of the repaint claim plus the owner of this manifest, together) or it needs a declaration form this table does not have.
_functions_excluded.obv: CUMULATIVE FROM THE FIRST BAR, WITH NO ABSOLUTE SEED. On-Balance Volume at bar i is the signed sum of every volume since the series began, so its LEVEL is a fact about where the fetch started rather than about the market — hand it 500 bars and 5,000 and the same date reads two different numbers. No finite lookback bounds it and none of this table's declarations can say `all of it`, which is exactly `lesson_a_derived_value_must_not_depend_on_the_request`: a rolling value gets a warm-up prefix, a cumulative one needs an ABSOLUTE seed, and OBV has none. The CHART may draw it because a chart owns its whole window; a formula evaluated over a lookback-sized slice may not.
_functions_excluded.sar: STATEFUL, PATH-DEPENDENT, AND WITH NO PERIOD ARGUMENT TO DECLARE A WINDOW FROM. Parabolic SAR carries a trend flag, an extreme point and an acceleration factor forward from the first bar, and a MISSED TREND FLIP never decays out of the state the way an EMA's seed error does. So the value depends on the whole series, `step`/`max_step` are floats this table's only literal cannot express as arguments anyway, and any finite lookback would brand a number computed from a different history than the chart's. ⚠️ `compute_sar_events` is the alert-side reader and stays where it is — an EVENT column the alert catalog owns, not a function a formula composes.
_functions_excluded.vwap: SESSION-ANCHORED, SO ITS WINDOW IS A PROPERTY OF THE CLOCK AND NOT OF THE TREE. `computeVWAP` restarts at every ET calendar-day boundary, which means the bars it reads at bar i are `back to this session's open` — neither a constant nor a named argument, and it changes with the timeframe. Worse for this table specifically: deciding it needs the bar's TIMESTAMP, and `series` declares five fields and `t` is not one of them. Making vwap callable means either declaring the anchor as an argument kind this table does not have, or admitting a window `maxLookback` cannot sum — which is the trade `_no_offset` refuses on the owner's behalf.
_functions_excluded.macdSignal: ITS WINDOW IS `slow + signal`, A SUM OF TWO ARGUMENTS. Same shape as `adx`. ⭐ AND IT IS ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE, EXACTLY: the signal line is `ema(macd(close, 12, 26), 9)` and the histogram is `macd(close, 12, 26) - ema(macd(close, 12, 26), 9)`, because this table's `ema` and `indicator_compute._ema_core` seed identically (the SMA of the first full window, `k = 2/(n+1)`) and this table's `ema` restarts its seed on a NaN, which is exactly the compaction `compute_macd_raw` performs. The tree sum reads 26 + 9 = 35, which is one MORE than the true 34 — conservative, the direction a budget can use.
_functions_excluded.bbUpper: THE MULTIPLIER IS NOT A WHOLE NUMBER. This table declares two argument kinds and `int` is `a whole number of at least 1`, so a 1.5- or 2.5-sigma band is inexpressible and an `int`-only Bollinger would be a narrower indicator wearing the name. ⭐ AND THE MANIFEST ALREADY NAMES THE IDIOM: `sma(close, 20) + 2 * stdev(close, 20)` — see the note on `stdev`'s POPULATION divisor, which exists precisely so that expression draws the same band `computeBB` draws. Declaring `bbUpper` would put a second spelling AND a second implementation on one value.
_functions_excluded.bbMiddle: `sma(close, 20)`, spelled twice. The middle band IS the simple moving average — `computeBB` computes the same mean `sma` does — so a declaration here is a synonym, and a synonym computed by different code is the second-authority defect this table's header opens with.
_functions_excluded.bbLower: the mirror of `bbUpper`, refused for the same two reasons: `sma(close, 20) - 2 * stdev(close, 20)`.
_functions_excluded.stochD: ITS WINDOW IS `kPeriod + dPeriod`, A SUM OF TWO ARGUMENTS. ⭐ AND IT IS ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE: %D is the simple mean of %K over `dPeriod` and `compute_stoch_raw` computes it as exactly that, so `sma(stoch(high, low, close, 14), 3)` is the same column — pinned by the `stoch_d_by_composition` corpus case rather than asserted here.
_functions_excluded.changeN: 🔴 AN N-BAR CHANGE IS NOT `change`, AND A TRANSLATOR MUST REFUSE RATHER THAN TRUNCATE. Pine's `ta.change(src, n)` takes a period and appears in roughly a QUARTER of real scripts; this table's `change` declares `args: ["series"]` and `lookback: 1` and is one-bar ONLY. Mapping `ta.change(close, 5)` onto it returns a PLAUSIBLE WRONG NUMBER — the worst failure shape here — so the arity is the refusal: a translator reads `len(args) == 1` and declines. ⛔ WIDENING `change` TO `change(series, n)` WAS CONSIDERED AND REFUSED: it changes an EXISTING entry's arity, which moves the frozen `abs_change` conformance digest and silently re-means every stored formula that already calls it. An n-bar change belongs to whatever bounded backward-index form the owner of `_no_offset` eventually grants (`x - x[n]`), not to a quiet second arity on a shipped name.
_functions_excluded.hl2: ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE, AND A NAMED SYNONYM WOULD BE A SECOND SPELLING OF ONE VALUE: `(high + low) / 2`. The table's operators are the whole of what it needs, and `donchianMiddle(high, low, 1)` is the same number again by a third route — which is precisely why no entry is declared for it.
_functions_excluded.hlc3: ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE: `(high + low + close) / 3`. This is the TYPICAL PRICE `cci` and `mfi` compute internally, so a declared `hlc3` would also be a fourth place that formula lives.
_functions_excluded.variance: ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE: `stdev(x, n) * stdev(x, n)`. ⚠️ AND THE DIVISOR IS THE POINT — this table's `stdev` is the POPULATION deviation (divisor `n`), stated where it is implemented and matched in both lanes, so the square of it is the POPULATION variance. A declared `variance` computed independently would be one refactor away from disagreeing with the `stdev` it is supposed to be the square of.
_functions_excluded.cross: ALREADY EXPRESSIBLE: `crossOver(a, b) || crossUnder(a, b)`. ⚠️ The `||` is the table's logical OR over a 0/1 column (`_booleans`), so the result is 0/1/NaN exactly as each half is — a declared `cross` would have to reproduce that domain and could get it wrong.
_functions_excluded._ichimokuSpanA_note: NOT EXCLUDED — declared above. It is listed here only to record that its window is `max(tenkan, kijun)` in the textbook and `senkouB` in the shipped implementation, and the shipped one is what `arg4` declares.
_functions_excluded._ichimoku_forward_cloud: THE STANDARD 26-BAR FORWARD DISPLACEMENT OF THE CLOUD IS NOT DRAWN BY THIS PRODUCT AND IS THEREFORE NOT DECLARABLE. `indicators.js` records the deviation deliberately (`spanA`/`spanB` sit over the price that produced them, not 26 bars ahead) and `compute_ichimoku_raw` mirrors it. Declaring `forward: arg3` on the two spans would brand them `preview-repaints` for a displacement the compute does not perform — a badge describing maths that does not run. ⭐ `ichimokuChikou` IS declared with a `forward`, because that one really does read `close[j + kijun]`, and it is the table's first and only entry whose repaint verdict is `preview-repaints` rather than `non-repainting`.
_functions_excluded._adx_was_here: ADX WAS EXCLUDED HERE UNTIL 2026-08-11, and the reason it gave was correct at the time: ITS WINDOW IS `2 * period` AND THIS TABLE CANNOT SAY THAT. The table can say it now — `lookback` accepts a whole multiple of an argument (`2*arg3`), mirrored in both lanes and measured by tests/test_ast_lookback_parity.py. The second half of the old note still stands and is why `adx` BINDS the shipped computeADX/compute_adx_raw rather than being composed: ADX smooths DX with Wilder's k = 1/n and this table's `ema` is k = 2/(n+1), so an expansion would have been a look-alike.

_scalars_excluded.ticker: the row's IDENTITY, not a value a formula reads. `ticker == "AAPL"` needs a string literal and this table's only literal is a number
_scalars_excluded.company: TEXT. A name is not a number and the table declares no string literal, so no expression over it is writeable
_scalars_excluded.sector: TEXT, and the one exclusion a user will feel. `sector == "Technology"` is INEXPRESSIBLE here -- granting it means string literals in the parser, both interpreters, the linter and the read-back, which is a phase of its own. Sector filtering stays in the classic screener UI
_scalars_excluded.industry: TEXT, for the same reason as `sector`
_scalars_excluded.exchange: TEXT, for the same reason as `sector`
_scalars_excluded.ma_stack: TEXT -- a rendered arrangement of moving averages, not a magnitude. The individual distances are declared as scalars instead
_scalars_excluded.candle_type: TEXT -- a classification label. The measured components (body, wicks, close position) are declared as scalars instead
_scalars_excluded.patterns: a comma-joined LIST, not a scalar. Expressing membership needs a `contains` this table does not declare; `pattern_conf_max` is the numeric part and IS declared
_scalars_excluded.snapshot_date: an `as_of` SOURCE. Declaring it as a scalar would let a formula compute on its own freshness stamp -- and it is TEXT besides
_scalars_excluded.bars_asof: the same, for the bar-dated family
_scalars_excluded.built_at: an operations timestamp. It dates the WRITE, not the value, so a formula reading it would be screening on when the builder ran

_functions_math: SQR/LOG/CLG/EXP/SGN, the three math operators and the trig family are all POINTWISE: lookback 0, no state, no warm-up, and they cannot repaint. DOMAIN REFUSALS ANSWER NaN, NEVER AN EXCEPTION AND NEVER A SUBSTITUTE VALUE -- sqrt of a negative, log of a non-positive and MOD/idiv by zero are all 'not computable', which is exactly what NaN already means everywhere else in this table. A scan that asked for LOG(C) on a zero close gets a bar it cannot answer for, not a -inf that would then compare as the smallest thing in the universe and silently win every < test.
_functions_sum_dev: `sum` and `dev` are the two rolling reductions TradingView scripts reach for most after the averages. ⛔ `dev` is Pine's `ta.dev`: the MEAN ABSOLUTE DEVIATION about the simple average of the same window -- NOT the standard deviation, which this table already declares as `stdev`. They differ on every real series, and CCI is defined on the mean absolute one: mapping `dev` to `stdev` would return a plausible CCI that is wrong on every bar, which is the exact failure the PCF look-alike table exists to prevent.
